papers.title: Pathogenicity and virulence of Giardia intestinalis .
papers.abstract: Giardiasis, caused by Giardia intestinalis , is a prevalent intestinal protozoan infection worldwide. Clinical manifestations are variable, and many infections remain asymptomatic. Disease pathogenesis is multifactorial, involving brush border enzyme deficiency, apoptosis, dysbiosis and increased intestinal permeability. Advances in genomics, genetic tools, and model systems have substantially improved our understanding of the parasite's virulence mechanisms. Giardia exhibits considerable genetic diversity, with distinct assemblages associated with differences in parasite biology. Attachment is mediated by the ventral disk, while the parasite's eight flagella contribute to motility and intestinal persistence. Antigenic variation of cysteine-rich surface proteins enables immune evasion and promotes chronic infection, but the level of inflammation is low. The parasite releases a variety of proteins and extracellular vesicles containing proteins and small RNAs that play important roles in host-cell interactions and modulation of the gut microbiome. This review describes areas that need further research to connect pathogenesis to specific virulence mechanisms.

papers.title: Evaluation of six generative large language models answering pre-analytical questions in medical microbiology.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have the potential to be integrated into diagnostics workflows, yet their reliability in pre-analytical diagnostic stewardship remains uncertain. We aimed to evaluate the performance of six LLMs answering common pre-analytical questions in the domain of medical microbiology. Next, we propose a blueprint to evaluate LLMs in medical microbiology. We compared general-purpose models from OpenAI (GPT-3.5, GPT-4) and Meta AI (Llama2-7B, Llama2-13B), alongside two domain-enhanced versions (customised GPT-4 agent and Llama2-7B Medical) in a hybrid evaluation framework. First, we quantified the response length (word count), then assessed the similarity between LLM-generated responses and expert-reviewed reference answers (BLEU/ROUGE scores, BERTScore). Finally, thirty-three medical professionals rated the accuracy and completeness of the LLM-generated responses on a 1-7-point scale. Responses of OpenAI models showed greater similarity to the reference set and significantly outperformed Meta AI-based models in accuracy and completeness. The customized generative pre-trained transformer (GPT) matched performance of OpenAI's general-purpose models, while generating significantly shorter responses (p<0.001). Quality ratings varied markedly between professionals, as medical microbiologists and experienced infectious disease specialists assigned significantly lower scores compared to infectious disease trainees and medical students (p<0.001). We observed considerable variation in LLM performance and highlight differences in perceived response quality across professional groups, emphasizing the need for critical appraisal when consulting LLMs for pre-analytical guidance.

papers.title: Surveillance, genetic diversity, and virulence characterisation of Francisella halioticida in blue mussels from the United Kingdom and Ireland.
papers.abstract: Francisella halioticida is a recently recognized pathogen affecting molluscs. In Europe, its presence has been documented within mussel populations in both France and England. At present, data concerning its genetic variability in mussels remain scarce. Between 2024 and 2025, a comprehensive monitoring programme was implemented to assess F. halioticida prevalence in southern England, alongside analyses of archived samples from Scotland and Ireland. The findings indicated a low prevalence of the pathogen within the surveyed populations, primarily associated with mild or localized infections. Phylogenetic analyses based on multi-locus sequence analysis showed genetic variability of F. halioticida in mussels across surveyed locations and years, however a distinct F. halioticida cluster from mussels separated from F. halioticida infecting scallops and abalone was identified. A F. halioticida metagenome assembled genome was obtained from an infected mussel from southern England, with 3666 predicted ORFs, and a ~14.2 kb region containing a putative Francisella Pathogenicity Island, including genes associated with Type VI secretion system components (TssK, DotU, IglE, and IglH), together with several hypothetical proteins, and flanked by IS3 family transposases. Additional virulence-associated genes were detected, including transcriptional and global regulators, oxidative stress and detoxification genes, and metallopeptidases. These findings improve understanding of the occurrence, diversity, and genomic features of F. halioticida in wild mussel populations, highlighting the need for expanded surveillance and higher-resolution genomic data to better understand its epidemiology and pathogenic potential. This improved resolution enhances risk assessment, enables early detection of emerging lineages, and supports more targeted monitoring strategies for wild mussel populations.

papers.title: The Emergence and Spread of Third-generation Cephalosporin-Resistant Neisseria Meningitidis in China.
papers.abstract: Neisseria meningitidis is the causative agent of invasive meningococcal disease. Although third-generation cephalosporins remain the recommended empirical therapy, there has been a growing number of globally reported isolates with resistance. This study aims to elucidate the genetic and evolutionary mechanisms underlying third-generation cephalosporin resistance in N. meningitidis. Whole-genome sequencing and phenotypic antibiotic susceptibility testing were performed, and the potential resistance determinants, genomic features, and evolutionary trajectories of resistant strains were comprehensively characterized. Seven PBP2 mutation sites potentially associated with resistance were identified, including A311V, R468K, E469K, D/N472E, L/P480A, T483S, and G545S. Genomic analysis revealed that strains possessing these seven potential resistance determinant mutations emerged within the past two decades and exhibited an increasing trend. The majority of these strains were isolated from northern regions of China. The predominant mutation strains were located in mainly epidemic strains, like cc4821, cc23, serogroup B and serogroup Y, respectively. Systematic phylogenetic analysis revealed that there has been a phenomenon of cross-regional transmission. Three potential cross-regional transmission third-generation cephalosporin-resistant strain types were identified, namely cc4821-ST-8920-NEIS1753_3923-penA795, ST-14760-NEIS1753_3652-penA1357, and cc23-ST-18108-NEIS1753_5058-penA1258. This study systematically analyzed the phenotypic and genetic characteristics of third-generation cephalosporin-resistant N. meningitidis strains. It not only deepened the understanding of the resistance mechanism but also provided a scientific basis and practical guidance for rapid clinical detection, laboratory monitoring, as well as the prevention and control of cross-regional transmission risks.

papers.title: Genomic ascertainment of systemic autoinflammatory diseases: a retrospective cohort study in two population-based biobanks.
papers.abstract: Systemic autoinflammatory diseases are rare diseases caused by innate immune dysregulation and are often linked to single-gene variants. Diagnosis remains challenging due to incomplete penetrance and variable expressivity. This study aimed to quantify the prevalence, penetrance, and clinical spectrum of systemic autoinflammatory diseases associated with pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in 28 genes. This retrospective cohort study applied a genome-first approach to whole exome sequencing linked to electronic health records from Geisinger MyCode Community Health Initiative (USA) and the UK Biobank (UK). From a curated list of 27 dominantly inherited and one acquired disease gene, individuals with autosomal dominant pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants or somatic pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants of UBA1 were classified as cases. Variants were classified according to American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics guidelines and assigned to tier 1 or tier 2. Controls were participants without any pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant in the 28 genes. Penetrance (≥1 systemic autoinflammatory disease-associated ICD-10 code group) and clinical spectrum were assessed in tier 1 cases by comparing inflammatory ICD-10 codes and immunosuppressant use between cases and controls, with expressivity defined as the number of enriched ICD-10 code groups. Odds ratios (ORs) were calculated using Fisher's exact test with Bonferroni-Holm correction, and cohorts were analysed separately. There was no lived experience involvement in the study design or conduct. The final dataset consisted of 640 092 participants (170 503 from Geisinger MyCode and 469 589 from the UK Biobank). 280 958 (43·9%) were male and 359 134 (56·1%) were female. We identified 159 individuals carrying rare pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in 17 genes, corresponding to a prevalence of 0·04% (63 of 170 503) in Geisinger MyCode and 0·02% (96 of 469 589) in the UK Biobank with a combined estimated prevalence of one in 4026 individuals (0·02%). Only one participant had a documented diagnosis of an autoinflammatory disorder. Geisinger MyCode cases had a disease penetrance of 79% (50 of 63) compared with a disease penetrance of 32% (31 of 96) in the UK Biobank. Overall, disease penetrance was 51%, with 81 of 159 cases exhibiting inflammatory features across multiple organ systems, especially pulmonary and cutaneous manifestations, as well as diagnoses of vasculitis (Geisinger MyCode OR 5·06 [1·01-15·54]) and rheumatic autoimmune disorders (Geisinger MyCode OR 2·29 [0·88-5·04]; UK Biobank OR 12·28 [4·12-30·68]. We also observed increased use of immunosuppressive medications in cases compared to controls (Geisinger MyCode OR 3·98 [95% CI 1·40-9·23]) consistent with clinically relevant disease. These findings suggest that monogenic autoinflammatory diseases are more common than currently recognised. Despite carrying disease-associated variants, almost no affected individuals had a documented systemic autoinflammatory disease diagnoses, pointing to a substantial gap in disease recognition and a missed opportunity to identify individuals with systemic inflammation who could benefit from genetic evaluation to guide therapy. Division of Cancer Epidemiology and Genetics, National Cancer Institute, the National Institutes of Health.

papers.title: Single-cell CRISPR screen maps epigenetic regulators of lineage specification and malignancies in human HSPCs.
papers.abstract: Mapping how genetic perturbations influence cell fate is key to understanding human development and disease. Here, we developed a massively parallel single-cell CRISPR (scCRISPR) screening platform in primary human hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs), profiling 322 regulators across 172,382 single-perturbed cells. The resulting multi-layered regulatory framework captured known associations and enabled functional annotation of regulator-phenotype relationships. Specifically, our atlas revealed that regulators acted within perturbation clusters to govern distinct gene programs that shaped cell fate. As proof of concept, we illustrated several examples. SMYD3 emerged as a negative regulator of long-term regenerative capacity. Analysis of lineage output further identified KMT5B, TRIM24, SETD7, and NSD3 as regulators associated with lineage-biased outputs. Finally, integration with clinical datasets identified PRDM10 as a candidate dependency in acute myeloid leukemia (AML). This work establishes a scalable functional genomics platform in a primary human stem cell system.

papers.title: Molecular mechanisms and regulatory networks governing Yersinia biofilm formation and host adaptation.
papers.abstract: The genus Yersinia includes three human pathogens- Y . pestis , Y. pseudotuberculosis , and Y. enterocolitica -where biofilm formation plays distinct roles in transmission and environmental persistence. All three species share the core biofilm machinery-the hmsHFRS operon, encoding enzymes for poly-β-1,6-N-acetylglucosamine (PNAG) exopolysaccharide production, and the c-di-GMP signaling controlling this production-but their regulatory networks and biofilm outputs differ. Transcriptional control of hms involves an integrated network that includes the Rcs phosphorelay (reshaped by rcsA pseudogenization), PhoP/PhoQ, EnvZ/OmpR, BarA/UvrY, Fur/Zur, CRP-cAMP, RovM/RovA, and multiple sigma factors. Post-transcriptionally, the Hfq-sRNA and CsrA-CsrB/CsrC systems modulate gene expression; the latter is directly validated in Y. pestis and Y. pseudotuberculosis , whereas its role in Y. enterocolitica is inferred from genomic conservation. At the translational and enzymatic levels, polyamines sustain Hms protein production, while redox signals govern the HmsC-HmsD disulfide switch, controlling diguanylate cyclase activity. This multi-layer architecture ensures that biofilm output is tuned to species-specific ecological niches. In host adaptation, Y. pestis transitioned from a foodborne enteric pathogen to a flea-borne lifestyle through key genetic events-acquisition of ymt , pseudogenization of rcsA , inactivation of y2909 / y3389, and ureD -which are not shared with Y. pseudotuberculosis or Y. enterocolitica , thereby explaining their different biofilm-dependent transmission strategies. Studies in Caenorhabditis elegans have identified host O-glycosylation modifications as receptors for biofilm attachment. This review summarizes progress on the molecular mechanisms, regulatory networks, and host-adaptive functions of Yersinia biofilm formation and proposes future research directions to address knowledge gaps. Future priorities include the identification of c-di-GMP effectors, flea-specific signals, 3D biofilm imaging, and CRISPR-based detection.

papers.title: Letters and Biological Process: Linguistic Structure Encodes Hierarchical Depth in the Gene Ontology.
papers.abstract: We asked whether the natural language used to name Gene Ontology (GO) Biological Process terms encodes hierarchical position in the GO directed acyclic graph. Semantic representations of term names, combined with UMAP visualization and k-means clustering (k=20) recovered biologically coherent semantic groups whose depth distributions differed strongly (Kruskal-Wallis H=5244, p<10-300; η2=0.217). Term-name length increased with depth (Pearson r=0.34, Spearman ρ=0.37; slope ≈3.2 letters per level), and this positive scaling held under shortest-, longest-, and average-path depth definitions. Vocabulary entropy followed a bell-shaped diversification-specialization curve with an intermediate-depth peak (maximal at depth 4) that lies outside a Monte Carlo null envelope across most depths, and null-model tests supported a genuine linguistic-hierarchical association. The go_lingdepth Python package, regenerated result tables, and figure-generation scripts are available at https://github.com/Sadiya-ISU/Letters-and-Biological-Process and archived on Zenodo (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.21501473). Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

papers.title: Ketamine administered biomedically or as psychedelic-assisted therapy in treatment-resistant depression: Differing efficacy based on depressive subtype or presence of childhood trauma?
papers.abstract: ObjectiveThe ideas presented in this paper are based on a presentation at a festschrift event marking the retirement of Professor Gordon Parker from UNSW, Sydney. Drawing on Gordon's depressive subtyping approach and his critiques of a unitary view of major depressive disorder and treatment-resistant depression (TRD), we aim to (i) explore differing models of ketamine for TRD - biomedical versus 'psychedelic-assisted' therapy, and (ii) whether there may be differential efficacy in each approach based on subtype and/or childhood trauma.ConclusionPreliminary results from our study indicate in an open-label (but not randomised controlled) setting, biomedical ketamine may be superior in melancholic versus non-melancholic depression subtyped using Sydney Melancholia Prototypic Index. Studies of ketamine as a psychedelic agent combined with psychotherapy are lacking. We outline an empirical approach to determine whether ketamine with integrated psychotherapy has differential efficacy based on depressive subtype or past childhood trauma.

papers.title: Field Performance and usability of a novel molecular point-of-care assay for C hlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae detection.
papers.abstract: BackgroundFew studies have evaluated the field performance of novel point-of-care molecular assays for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae . We aimed to assess the performance, feasibility and acceptability of the prototype OraSure CT/NG assay (InteliQuick, OraSure Technologies Inc., USA) among clinics in Peru.MethodsBetween May and June 2025, we recruited men and women from three clinics in Lima. Participants self-collected rectal and vaginal or penile meatal swabs and provided urine samples, while clinic staff collected pharyngeal swabs. We compared results of the prototype OraSure CT/NG assay with reference testing using the Xpert CT/NG assay (Cepheid, USA) on rectal, pharyngeal, and vaginal swabs as well as male urine, and the Aptima Combo 2 CT/NG assay (Hologic, USA) on penile meatal swabs and male urine. We applied an intention-to-diagnose framework, calculating explanatory scientific accuracy, which permits repeat testing on invalid specimens, and pragmatic application accuracy which classifies invalid results as false positives or negatives. We calculated the positive (PPA) and negative percent agreement (NPA) for each anatomic site and used closed-ended surveys to assess acceptability and feasibility among laboratory personnel.ResultsWe enrolled 157 participants. Of 470 specimens tested by the OraSure CT/NG assay, 92.3% yielded a valid result on the first attempt (99.1% after repeated testing). Among symptomatic participants, PPA for N. gonorrhoeae was 100.0% (penile meatal), 72.7% (pharyngeal), and 69.2% (rectal), while for C. trachomatis the PPA was 50.0% (penile meatal), 33.3% (pharyngeal), and 85.7% (rectal). NPA remained >90% across all sites. Seven of eight clinic laboratory personnel rated the assay as easy to use and compatible with existing clinic workflows.ConclusionsThe OraSure CT/NG assay showed consistently high NPA and was acceptable to users, while the PPA varied by pathogen and specimen type.

papers.title: A PNA-assisted magnetic bead-confined CbAgo-CRISPR/Cas12a cascade for amplification-free detection of Mycobacterium avium subsp. paratuberculosis F57 DNA.
papers.abstract: Mycobacterium avium subsp. paratuberculosis (MAP), the causative agent of Johne's disease in ruminants, has attracted increasing attention because of its potential zoonotic relevance. Sensitive molecular detection of MAP typically relies on nucleic acid amplification to overcome low pathogen abundance; however, amplification may generate nonspecific products and false-positive results. Here, targeting MAP-specific F57 double-stranded DNA, we developed a peptide nucleic acid (PNA)-assisted, magnetic bead-confined Clostridium butyricum Argonaute (CbAgo)-CRISPR/Cas12a cascade electrochemiluminescent (ECL) biosensing platform for amplification-free MAP detection. The platform comprises two functional magnetic-bead microreactors. In the PNA-CbAgo cleavage microreactor (PCCM), PNA and CbAgo/gDNA complexes are co-immobilized on magnetic beads. PNA-mediated local duplex opening facilitates CbAgo cleavage and generation of target-derived DNA fragments (tDNA). In the CRISPR/Cas12a-Ru ECL signaling microreactor (CREM), CRISPR/Cas12a-crRNA complexes and Ru-labeled ssDNA reporters are co-confined on magnetic beads. The generated tDNA activates localized CRISPR/Cas12a trans -cleavage, leading to reporter release and a target-dependent decrease in ECL intensity. Mechanistic studies showed that the PCCM enhances tDNA generation through PNA-assisted duplex opening and bead interfacial confinement, whereas the CREM enables efficient ECL transduction through localized CRISPR/Cas12a-crRNA-reporter coupling. Under optimized conditions, the platform achieved a detection limit of 34.1 CFU mL -1 , exhibited good specificity, agreed well with qPCR in spiked bovine fecal samples, and demonstrated robust overall performance in complex matrices. This work provides an amplification-free ECL strategy for sensitive and specific MAP detection and highlights the potential of bead-confined programmable nuclease cascades for pathogen nucleic acid analysis.

papers.title: PgaR is a positive regulator of the pgaABCD biosynthetic operon in Klebsiella pneumoniae.
papers.abstract: The biosynthetic locus encoding the exopolysaccharide poly-N-acetyl-glucosamine (PNAG) is widely conserved across bacteria, including the World Health Organization critical-priority pathogen Klebsiella pneumoniae (Kp). In Kp, PNAG synthesis is mediated by the pgaABCD operon, yet its lineage-specific regulation remains incompletely understood. Using a comparative genomics approach to interrogate the pgaABCD locus across the high-risk clonal Kp complex 258 (CC258) lineage, we identified a previously uncharacterized positive transcriptional regulator located immediately upstream of pgaA , which we designate pgaR . Phylogenetic analysis revealed recurrent evolutionary events affecting this regulatory region, including repeated deletion or truncation of pgaR and a G > A substitution upstream of the pgaR start codon. Functional characterization demonstrated that loss of pgaR abolishes pgaABCD expression and PNAG production, whereas the upstream G > A substitution drives PNAG hyperproduction. Under in vitro growth conditions, Kp produce extensive extracellular PNAG networks. Using a prototype hypervirulent strain to model the role of PNAG in vivo indicated that it is dispensable for virulence in murine pneumonia and peritonitis models. In contrast, PNAG hyper-production significantly attenuated virulence and reduced disease severity. Collectively, these findings identify PgaR as a novel upstream gene regulator of the pgaABCD operon and reveal a previously unrecognized lineage-specific layer of PNAG regulation in Kp. This demonstrates that opposing PNAG phenotypes, loss and hyper-production, have independently and repeatedly emerged among clinical CC258 isolates, highlighting selective pressures acting on this locus.

papers.title: Host- and pathogen-regulated exocytosis facilitates dynamic distribution of endolysosomal content during infection by the vacuolar pathogen Coxiella burnetii .
papers.abstract: Coxiella burnetii is an obligate intracellular bacterial pathogen that causes the zoonotic disease Q fever. Coxiella extensively subverts host vesicle traffic and replicates within lysosome-derived, spacious vacuoles by secreting a suite of effectors through the type IVB secretion system (T4BSS). This study investigates the regulation and role of a fundamental lysosomal process, exocytosis, in the prolonged maintenance of Coxiella vacuolar niche. Biochemical, microscopic, and proteomic approaches indicate that infection promotes release of extracellular vesicles (EVs). Increase in extracellular levels of endolysosomal proteins and surface localization of LAMP1 were identified in both phagocytic and non-phagocytic cells, during later stages of infection. Interestingly, infection-induced exocytosis was dependent on the activity of the bacterial T4BSS. On one hand, knockdown of the lysosomal master transcriptional regulator TFEB significantly reduces basal exocytosis and enhances intracellular Coxiella replication, while deficiency of the exocytosis-associated SNARE, Syntaxin 11, does not reduce basal exocytosis and yet, increases Coxiella replication, suggesting that host exocytosis is not the sole or a dominant determinant of the infection process. On the other hand, modulating the activity of a key host exocytosis regulator- the calcium channel TRPML1, decreases intracellular Coxiella replication suggesting a tightly regulated role of TRPML1. Infection was also associated with the extracellular detection of LAMP1-associated Coxiella , suggesting an encased egress mechanism. Together, this study demonstrates that Coxiella infection activates exocytosis in a temporal, host-, and bacterial factor-dependent manner.

papers.title: A plasmid-encoded T3SS underlies the virulence of enteropathogenic Providencia alcalifaciens strains isolated from a large foodborne outbreak in Japan.
papers.abstract: Providencia alcalifaciens is a gut commensal bacterium and also an emerging enteric pathogen associated with sporadic infections and outbreak cases in humans. The most notable outbreak caused by this bacterium occurred in 1996 in Fukui Prefecture, Japan, affecting 270 individuals. However, the pathogenic mechanisms responsible for this outbreak remain unknown. In this study, we identified the key virulence determinants of the Fukui outbreak strains through genomic and functional analyses. These strains uniquely carry a ~162 kb large plasmid encoding a type III secretion system (T3SS) closely homologous to the Salmonella SPI-1 T3SS. We also show that the plasmid-encoded T3SS (T3SSp) constitutes a functional secretion system and is essential for the pathogenicity of the Fukui outbreak strain, including the invasion of cultured epithelial cells and the induction of diarrhea in a rabbit model. Secretome analysis identified effectors secreted in a T3SSp-dependent manner, among which PipA-sharing limited sequence similarity with SipA, a SPI-1 T3SS effector-plays a crucial role in inducing diarrhea. Ectopic expression of PipA in HeLa cells caused focal accumulation of F-actin, indicating its cytoskeleton-modulating activity. Comparative genomics with other Providencia species revealed the dissemination of the large plasmid, with structural variations among enteropathogenic strains of P. alcalifaciens and Providencia rustigianii associated with clinical cases in humans and animals. Thus, our findings underscore the molecular basis of P. alcalifaciens pathogenicity in the Fukui outbreak and highlight the significance of the large plasmids encoding T3SS in driving pathogenic evolution among Providencia species.

papers.title: Multiplex digital PCR for rapid quantitative detection and dynamic monitoring of respiratory pathogens in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid.
papers.abstract: Lower respiratory tract infections (LRTIs) remain a leading cause of mortality worldwide. Rapid and comprehensive etiological diagnosis is critical yet challenging: existing approaches, from culture to multiplex PCR and mNGS, carry distinct limitations in one or more of turnaround time, sensitivity, cost, or quantitative resolution. We developed a 33-plex digital PCR (dPCR) assay for absolute quantification of bacteria, viruses, fungi, and atypical pathogens in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF). Systematic evaluation of five liquefaction protocols identified dithiothreitol (DTT) as the optimal universal pretreatment, ensuring balanced RNA and DNA recovery. The assay demonstrated reliable quantification from 10 to 10 5 copies per test for all 33 targets ( R 2 > 0.99), with 27 targets showing linearity across full range and 6 targets exhibiting linearity from 10 to 10 4 copies per test (10 5 as upper detection limit). The limit of detection was 5 copies per test for all targets. In 105 BALF samples, dPCR achieved a significantly higher positive rate than culture (96.19% vs. 83.81%, p < 0.05), particularly for polymicrobial infections (85.71% vs. 40.00%). Concordance with mNGS for primary pathogens was 86.96% (20/23) for 14 primary pathogens across 23 positive samples. The complete workflow from sample pre-treatment to results required only 2.5 hours. Serial BALF dPCR quantification of P. aeruginosa and K. pneumoniae in one severe LRTI case tracked pathogen loads in parallel with clinical course and antibiotic responses, preliminarily supporting the technical feasibility of dynamic monitoring. This study demonstrates the feasibility of a rapid 33-plex dPCR assay for comprehensive respiratory pathogen profiling in BALF, with potential for dynamic monitoring in critically ill patients.

papers.title: Diagnostic performance of sexually transmitted infection screening in men with sterile leukocyturia detected by flow cytometry.
papers.abstract: Sexually transmitted infections (STIs) have increased in recent years, especially amongst young men. However, genitourinary symptoms continue to be initially managed as a urinary tract infection. The aim of this study was to evaluate the diagnostic yield of STI screening in urine samples submitted for culture from men with sterile leukocyturia and to assess the discriminative ability of leukocyturia for detecting STIs. A prospective study (June 2019-May 2024) was conducted using midstream urine samples from men aged 15-59 years with leukocyturia ≥20 leukocytes/μL detected by flow cytometry (UF-1000i and UF-5000i, Sysmex®) and negative urine culture. STI detection was performed using multiplex PCR (Allplex™ STI Essential Assay, Seegene). Demographic variables and leukocyturia were analyzed. A total of 495 samples were included, with STIs diagnosed in 201 (40.6%). Chlamydia trachomatis was the most frequently detected pathogen (59.7%). Diagnostic yield was similar in Primary Care and the Emergency Department (41.6% vs 37.6%). Patients with STIs were younger (29 vs. 35 years; p< 0.001) and more frequently of foreign origin (51.6% vs. 35.3%; p< 0.001). Leukocyturia was higher in STI-positive than STI-negative samples [median (IQR): 358 (110-959) vs. 85 (35-315) WBC/μL; p < 0.001], mainly due to Neisseria gonorrhoeae [median (IQR): 1264 (690-3526) WBC/μL]. Opportunistic STI screening in men with sterile leukocyturia showed a high diagnostic yield and supports the systematic inclusion of molecular STI testing in this population. However, the discriminative ability of leukocyturia was limited.
authors: José Luis Díaz de Tuesta Del Arco

papers.title: Individual susceptibility to disgust modulates neural and systemic immune responses to virtual infections.
papers.abstract: Disgust is a key psychological mechanism for avoiding pathogen exposure and constitutes a central component of the behavioral immune system. While disgust is thought to reduce infection risk through avoidance, it remains unclear how individual differences in disgust sensitivity shape downstream neuroimmune responses to perceived pathogen threats. Here, we show that lower disgust sensitivity is associated with stronger activation of type 1 innate lymphoid cells during exposure to infectious, compared with neutral, avatars in virtual reality. Disgust sensitivity further correlated with circulating signaling factors involved in immune regulation, including hormones related to the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, and eicosanoids. Linear models incorporating disgust sensitivity and threat exposure predicted these signaling factors, which in turn enabled accurate prediction of type 1 innate lymphoid cells responses using a pretrained neural network. Recreating this putative pathway, we were able to predict immune responses solely by disgust scores. Additionally, resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging revealed that exposure to infectious avatars altered hypothalamic connectivity with brain regions involved in visual processing, peripersonal space representation, and social cognition, and these effects were modulated by individual disgust sensitivity. Together, these findings suggest that disgust sensitivity modulates multiple levels of the neuroimmune response to perceived pathogen threats. Across two complementary experiments, our results are consistent with a model linking sensory threat detection, hypothalamic signaling, and systemic immune activation. Rather than uniformly amplifying immune responses, higher disgust sensitivity appears to bias pathogen defense toward neural processing, whereas lower disgust sensitivity is associated with stronger physiological immune activation.

papers.title: Real-World HRR Testing Pathways and Patterns of Detected Alterations in Prostate Cancer From the Multinational ARON-3 Study.
papers.abstract: Homologous recombination repair (HRR) testing is increasingly relevant in prostate cancer because it identifies patients who may benefit from biomarker-guided treatment strategies, including poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitors (PARPi). However, real-world implementation of HRR testing remains variable across countries and clinical settings, and the extent to which current testing pathways capture actionable alterations is not well defined. ARON-3 is a multinational, multicentre, retrospective real-world study of patients with prostate cancer. In this subanalysis, we assessed genomic testing uptake within the overall ARON-3 cohort and characterised HRR testing pathways and detected pathogenic alterations among patients with available genomic results. Genomic testing included germline, somatic tumour, and/or circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) assays performed in routine practice across participating centres. Multivariable logistic regression was used to identify clinicopathologic factors associated with undergoing genomic HRR testing. Among 2,192 patients included in ARON-3, genomic testing results were available for 719 (33%). Among tested patients, 660 (92%) underwent germline testing and 610 (85%) somatic testing; 549 (77%) underwent both, whereas 109 (15%) had germline-only and 61 (8%) somatic-only testing. In multivariable analysis, metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer, high-volume disease, and Gleason score > 8 were independently associated with higher odds of testing, while age ≥ 70 years was associated with lower odds of testing. Overall, 238 tested patients (33%) harboured pathogenic HRR alterations, corresponding to 11% of the entire ARON-3 cohort. Somatic pathogenic alterations were more frequent than germline alterations. BRCA2 was the most frequently altered gene, while non-BRCA1/2 alterations were also detected, particularly in centres using broader multigene panels. Most centres relied on BRCA1/2-focused assays, and the use of liquid biopsy remained limited. This multinational real-world analysis demonstrates substantial heterogeneity in HRR testing uptake and testing pathways across participating ARON-3 centres. Testing was more commonly performed in patients with more advanced disease features, suggesting that clinically relevant subgroups may still be differentially selected for genomic assessment. Broader and more standardised implementation of comprehensive HRR profiling may improve the identification of actionable alterations and strengthen precision medicine in prostate cancer.

papers.title: Brought with the wind: A case of melioidosis acquired in the United States presenting with multiple pulmonary nodules.
papers.abstract: Burkholderia pseudomallei, the causative agent of melioidosis, is a gram-negative bacterium historically endemic to Southeast Asia and Northern Australia. However, recent environmental detection along the Gulf Coast and an increasing number of reported cases in non-travelers have raised questions regarding potential endemicity and environmental establishment in the Southern United States. We report a case of putatively locally acquired pulmonary melioidosis in a Florida resident with no recent international travel history, illustrating the diagnostic and therapeutic challenges posed by this rare pathogen. The patient presented with fever, pleuritic chest pain, and hypoxia following a period of severe weather. Computed tomography (CT) of the chest revealed multiple solid pulmonary nodules with ground-glass opacities and mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Given his underlying stage 3b chronic kidney disease (CKD), the patient was treated with an intensive course of intravenous ceftazidime followed by oral doxycycline monotherapy, achieving full clinical recovery. Follow-up imaging at 3 months demonstrated complete resolution of the pulmonary nodules. This case emphasizes the importance of considering melioidosis in the differential diagnosis for non-resolving community-acquired pneumonia or significant pulmonary nodules in the Southern United States, even in the absence of international travel. Risk factors such as diabetes mellitus and severe weather events are key clinical clues. While trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole remains the preferred eradication therapy, doxycycline may serve as a potential alternative for patients with renal impairment when first-line therapy is contraindicated.

papers.title: Molecular Detection of Anaplasma marginale in the Central Region of Venezuela: A PCR-based Assessment of the msp2 and msp5 Genes.
papers.abstract: Bovine anaplasmosis reduces livestock productivity in cattle, making timely and accurate diagnosis essential for epidemiological surveillance. To explore alternative primers for pathogen detection beyond the reference 19A/19B set targeting the single-copy msp5 gene and to update epidemiologic data we evaluated analytical and field performance of primers designed for the multicopy msp2 gene, using conserved terminal regions (msp2A/B). We also described the prevalence of A. marginale in specific sampled herds from several regions of Venezuela. PCR conditions were standardized, and the analytical sensitivity of msp2A/B and 19A/B was evaluated. Field evaluations involved 208 cattle from small farms in four distinct geographical regions of Venezuela (Aragua, Cojedes, Guárico, and Miranda), divided into two groups with different clinical characteristics. Both primer sets detected the pathogen at concentrations as low as 0.01 ng. In a herd of 24 cattle experiencing an anaplasmosis outbreak, positivity rates were 12.5% and 66.67% using primers msp2A/B and 19A/B, respectively. One of the positive field-sample amplicons was cloned and sequenced to confirm bacterial identity, yielding a 97% BLAST identity with complete coverage to the reference strain Florida. Additionally, 10 and 5 nucleotide substitutions were detected at the 5' and 3' ends, respectively, compared to the reference isolate. This suggests terminal heterogeneity in the gene that may contribute to the reduced diagnostic performance of msp2A/B. Additionally, 184 clinically healthy cattle analyzed solely with 19A/B revealed a subclinical prevalence of 41.85%. In a country with limited recent molecular reports, these findings underscore the epidemiological relevance of persistent infections. This study also constitutes the first report of an msp2 sequence from a Venezuelan A. marginale isolate, providing preliminary insights of the genetic diversity of A. marginale and support using msp5-based PCR for routine field detection and surveillance in Venezuela.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence in Prediction and Diagnosis of Fetal Growth Restriction: A Systematic Review.
papers.abstract: This systematic review evaluates evidence on artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) models for prediction and diagnosis of fetal growth restriction (FGR). The authors searched PubMed, Scopus, Embase, Web of Science, and Google Scholar, through June 2026 following PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Studies on AI/ML-based prediction or diagnosis techniques for FGR, Intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR) or Small for gestational age (SGA) fetuses. The prediction model risk of bias assessment Tool (PROBAST) was used to perform data extraction and risk of bias assessment. Twenty-seven studies were eligible for inclusion. AI applications were biophysical (n = 10), Doppler-based (n = 10), clinical (n = 7), ultrasound (n = 7), MRI (n = 7), radiomics imaging (n = 10), cardiotocography (n = 10), genomics (n = 10), and metabolomics-based biomarker models (n = 10). The model performance was good, with area under the receiver operating characteristic curves (AUC) of 0.71-0.91 and classification accuracies of 78.9-93.3%. Imaging and multimodal data-based models showed the highest predictive performance. The PROBAST assessment showed that the risk of bias was low for the participant, predictor and outcome domains, but the analytical domain raised methodological concerns; nine studies were low risk, 14 moderate and 4 high. The AI and ML models for FGR detection performed promisingly. Multimodal approaches that combine clinical, imaging and molecular data consistently outperform single modality models and constitute a major advance in precision obstetrics. However, there remains substantial heterogeneity, limited external validation and methodological issues. Future prospective multicenter studies, standardized reporting, and real-world implementation research are needed for routine clinical adoption.

papers.title: Innate and adaptive immunity pathways linking Mycoplasma pneumoniae to pediatric asthma phenotypes.
papers.abstract: Mycoplasma pneumoniae (Mp) is repeatedly detected during pediatric wheeze and asthma exacerbations, but its clinical significance depends on the host-response context. This review evaluates the clinical and mechanistic evidence linking Mp to pediatric asthma phenotypes and examines approaches for distinguishing biologically meaningful infection from incidental detection. We narratively synthesized clinical, experimental, immunological, toxin, and proteomic literature addressing Mp-associated wheeze, asthma exacerbation, epithelial injury, allergic amplification, and inflammatory endotyping. Evidence was distinguished by population and experimental system. Experimental studies show that Mp adheres to airway epithelium; disrupts mucociliary function; activates TLR2/TLR4, NF-κB, autophagy, and inflammasome pathways; and promotes cytokine networks that overlap with allergic asthma. In experimental allergic-airway models, epithelial alarmins, IgE responses, mast cells, and type 2 inflammation may amplify Mp-driven signals, whereas IL-23/IL-17 pathways recruit neutrophils and suggest mixed endotypes; altered corticosteroid responsiveness has not been established in pediatric Mp-associated asthma. CARDS toxin induces eosinophilic inflammation, mucus metaplasia, airway hyperresponsiveness, functional IgE responses, and worsening allergen-driven disease in experimental models. Upper-airway PCR positivity, however, may reflect carriage or prolonged detection rather than active lower-airway infection. Quantitative pathogen testing, paired serology, viral co-detection, age, atopy, microbiome context, and host-response biomarkers merit integrated evaluation in research. Proteomic and multi-omics signatures may support precision endotyping, improve causal attribution, and strengthen pediatric asthma trial design. Their diagnostic and treatment-predictive value remains unvalidated. • M. pneumoniae is linked to pediatric wheeze and asthma exacerbations, but upper-airway PCR may reflect carriage rather than active lower-airway infection. • Epithelial injury, type 2/Th17 responses, and CARDS toxin can promote asthma-like inflammation in experimental systems. • This review integrates diagnostic attribution, toxin biology, immune crosstalk, and proteomic endotyping in one pediatric framework. • It proposes an unvalidated combined pathogen-load and host-response assessment to investigate clinically meaningful M. pneumoniae-driven endotypes and guide trials.

papers.title: The influence of ergosterol on termites' defenses against Metarhizium infections.
papers.abstract: Termites respond to spores of pathogenic fungi that have adhered to the cuticle with brief bouts of rapid shaking, an alarm response that promotes allogrooming, which helps prevent fatal infections. The pathogen associated molecular pattern (PAMP) that elicits this proactive hygienic response is unknown. Ergosterol, an important component of the fungal cell membrane, has been identified as a potential PAMP in the subterranean termite Coptotermes formosansus. In this study, commercial or extracted ergosterol elicited a hygienic behavioral response in workers of the subterranean termite Reticulitermes flavipes. The ergosterol content of pathogenic spores of Metarhizium spp. were also found to vary among different strains and species of the fungus. However, there was a significant positive correlation between ergosterol content of different Metarhizium isolates and fatal infections caused by their spores (conidia). Alarm responses from challenges with conidia were not positively correlated with estimates of ergosterol content and instead were negatively correlated with ergosterol content although not significantly, which does not support the hypothesis that ergosterol is a critical recognition cue for the hygienic response. Termicin, an antifungal peptide in termite salivary secretions, was also most effective against the most lethal isolates, which had the highest ergosterol content. Ergosterol appears to influence spore membrane vulnerability to disruption by the antifungal peptide. Overall, our results indicate ergosterol influences both the vulnerability of Metarhizium conidia to termicin and the detection of an unidentified PAMP, which alerts termites to fungal contamination. This sets up a potential trade-off for the fungus between a shield for protection and signal for detection: reducing vulnerability to termicin by decreasing the content of cell membrane ergosterol results in an increase in a cell wall PAMP that termites can recognize and respond to with allogrooming. Reticulitermes spp. appear to have adaptively exploited this trade-off.

papers.title: [Advances in early bedside etiological diagnosis of severe pneumonia].
papers.abstract: The case fatality rate of severe pneumonia remains high, early and accurate etiological diagnosis is a prerequisite for precision antimicrobial therapy. Conventional culture techniques are limited by long turnaround times and low positivity rates. In recent years, novel detection systems such as microbiological rapid on-site evaluation(M-ROSE), point-of-care immunoloassays, multiplex PCR, and metagenomic sequencing have advanced rapidly, markedly shortening the time to pathogen identification. The integration of rapid detection assays for antimicrobial resistance genes has further facilitated precision antimicrobial therapy. Multi-omics analysis integrating the pathogen spectrum with host immune response status helps distinguish colonization from infection, thereby helping prevent antibiotic overuse. This article reviews techniques for pathogen and antimicrobial resistance gene detection together with strategies to distinguish colonization from infection to inform rapid bedside etiological diagnosis in severe pneumonia.

papers.title: Beyond genes and hotspots: Protein-informed interpretation of cancer mutations.
papers.abstract: Interpreting the biological and clinical significance of somatic mutations in cancer genomes remains challenging. In this issue of Cancer Cell, Hyeon et al. identify and map significantly mutated regions to protein domains and structural features, establishing a proteo-genomics framework for interpreting cancer mutations beyond genes and hotspots.

papers.title: Proteo-genomics-guided interpretation of somatic mutations in cancer genomes.
papers.abstract: Cancer genomes harbor hundreds of mutated genes, but their exact roles in tumorigenesis often remain incompletely understood. Here, by integrating protein structures with mutation data from 139,818 patients, we generate detailed, functional maps of mutations for 173 cancer genes in 18+ tumor types. In most cancer genes, oncogenic mutations accumulate in "significantly mutated regions" aligned with key functions, including DNA-binding domains in transcription factors (e.g., FOXA1), ligand-binding sites in receptors (e.g., ERBB2), catalytic domains in chromatin remodelers (e.g., EP300), substrate-recognition sites in ubiquitin-proteasome regulators (e.g., SPOP), and degradation signals in cell-cycle proteins (e.g., CCND1). In other cancer genes, mutations align more closely with constraints in three-dimensional protein structures, such as targeting the interior core (e.g., TP53) or a specific secondary structure (e.g., PTEN). Broadly, our study provides a proteo-genomic framework to characterize the effects of mutations in tumorigenesis and integrate them into workflows for clinical interpretation in precision medicine.

papers.title: Dual Host-Pathogen Screening of the Lung During Severe Influenza Using Spatial Transcriptomics.
papers.abstract: Here, we assessed whether spatially resolved capture of polyadenylated mRNA permitted simultaneous screening of host and viral responses in situ. Fresh-frozen lung samples from mice infected with H1N1 influenza A strain, PR8, were processed via genome-wide, spatial transcriptomics (ST) at 10-μm resolution. To determine if specific cell-types were detectable within the ST data, we first performed cellular deconvolution using publicly available, single-cell RNA-seq data of immune and non-immune cells from PR8-infected lungs. This revealed expected structures such as rings of epithelial cells lining airways, and at Day 10 post-infection (p.i.) unexpected structures dominated by B cells. We next screened ST data alone for groups of genes displaying similar spatial expression patterns. This again identified at Day 10 p.i. cellular aggregates enriched for genes associated with B cell biology. Mapping these gene signatures to a B cell transcriptomic atlas suggested plasmablasts had emerged early in the lung, which was confirmed by flow cytometry. Finally, by mapping ST data to the influenza A genome, we observed widespread expression of all 10 viral transcripts across samples at Day 4 but not Day 10 p.i., consistent with viral clearance. Cellular deconvolution analysis at Day 4 p.i. revealed proportions of every detected cell-type harbored viral transcripts, suggesting indiscriminate infection across the specific area of tissue examined. Subsequent whole-section immunohistochemical assessment further supported the phenomenon of localized indiscriminate infection, with these areas found adjacent to minimally infected zones. Thus, spatial screening of mRNA in tissues can simultaneously inform upon viral pathogenesis and host responses to infection.

papers.title: In silico subtractive genomics and reverse vaccinology approach reveal outer membrane proteins OMP47 and LptD as dual-purpose drug and vaccine targets in Pasteurella multocida Pm70
papers.abstract: Drug targets and vaccines for bacterial diseases are challenging to develop. Computational subtractive genomics and reverse vaccinology offer a viable substitute for conventional drug and vaccine development approaches. In recent years, Pasteurella multocida, a Gram-negative pathogen responsible for severe infections in humans along with major diseases in livestock and poultry, has developed resistance to multiple drugs. As a result, there is an urgent demand for research into reliable, efficient, highly potent, and cost-effective strategies to combat the rise of Pasteurella multocida infections. To address this, the present study integrated an in silico subtractive genomics and reverse vaccinology workflow to pinpoint proteins with potential value as both drug and vaccine targets. From the complete Pasteurella multocida Pm70 proteome, we identified 446 proteins that had no similarities with human proteins, out of which 129 were found to be essential for the pathogens survival. These 129 proteins are therefore potential candidates for drug development. Further metabolic pathway analysis, virulence potential, subcellular localization, and structural analyses revealed two outer membrane proteins, namely, 47 kDa outer membrane protein and lipopolysaccharide-assembly protein LptD, as promising candidates for therapeutic development. Subsequent antigenicity analysis revealed both outer membrane proteins as potential vaccine targets, exhibiting highly favorable antigenicity scores. Candidate B- and T-cell epitopes were systematically mapped from these two targets based on antigenicity, immunogenicity, toxicity, and allergenicity potential and only high-confidence epitopes were assembled using adjuvants and class-specific linkers to construct the final multi-epitope vaccine (MEV). The designed MEV construct was demonstrated to be highly antigenic, non-toxic and non-allergenic to humans, while possessing favorable structural and physicochemical properties, and exhibited strong binding interactions with human toll-like receptors with minimal molecular deformability. Although further experimental validation is recommended to fully assess their efficacy, the present study establishes a solid foundation for the development of novel therapeutics and vaccine candidates against P. multocida, ultimately contributing to the reduction of its rising infections.

papers.title: AI-Driven Design of Next-Generation Immunoinformatics Multi-Epitope Subunit Vaccine Targeting the Most Virulent Mpox Proteome: A Structural and Kinetic Validation Framework
papers.abstract: The resurgence of the Mpox virus (MPXV) highlights the urgent need for scalable, mutation-resistant countermeasures. Slow development timelines hinder traditional empirical vaccine discovery, while conventional vaccinology often yields high false-positive rates because it relies on static, linear sequence-based screening. These classical informatics filters consistently fail to predict physical structural stability or the dynamic presentation of immune cells under physiological conditions, creating a distinct translational gap between computational design and in vitro efficacy. To address these limitations, here we engineered an advanced, AI-augmented vaccine discovery pipeline targeting the most virulent components of the MPXV proteome. We systematically screened eight critical viral targets essential for replication, membrane morphogenesis, and host-cell entry to map highly conserved T-cell and B-cell epitopes. Moving beyond standard heuristic filtering, we implemented a high-fidelity deep learning validation layer: ESM-2 protein language models (pLMs) were deployed to calculate pseudo-perplexity scores across chimeric linker junctions (EAAAK, GPGPG) to guarantee structural naturalness, MHCflurry ensemble models successfully verified active intracellular antigen presentation, and structure-informed graph neural networks (GNNs) simulated the physical node-attention dynamics of the immune synapse. Finally, recurrent neural networks (RNNs)-driven mRNA kinetic modeling optimized translation initiation rates and minimum free energy profiles during in silico cloning. This multi-layered pipeline successfully yielded three structurally refined, multi-epitope vaccine constructs optimized for maximum global population coverage. ESM-2 structural validation confirmed exceptionally low perplexity scores at structural junctions, indicating that the engineered chimaeras have native-like stability and a minimized risk of proteolysis. GNN-based immune synapse modeling demonstrated highly stable binding kinetics and robust binding free energies between the target epitopes and human HLA alleles. Furthermore, RNN kinetic optimizations established that the cDNA sequences are optimized for high-yield expression in heterologous expression hosts without risk of ribosomal stalling or translational bottlenecks. This study establishes a deep learning-augmented framework that bridges the gap between theoretical sequence optimization and biopharmaceutical scalability. By validating the structural naturalness, real-world immunogenicity, and manufacturing kinetics of our vaccine chimeras, this framework presents a robust, proactive paradigm for rapid vaccine architecture against emerging orthopoxvirus threats.

papers.title: Tonotopic mapping in children shows an overrepresentation of high frequencies in autism
papers.abstract: Altered sensitivity to sounds despite normal peripheral hearing is common in neurodevelopmental disorders but the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here we investigate tonotopic organization in 86 children (6-11 years) with autism spectrum and related neurodevelopmental disorders as well as typically developing (TD) peers, using a child-friendly, passive listening, functional magnetic resonance imaging design. In TD children, tonotopic maps in primary auditory cortex resembled the typical high-low-high frequency gradients previously reported in adults, while children with autism showed an overrepresentation of high frequencies consistent with what has been observed in animal models of autism. Higher frequency tuning further correlated with greater caregiver-reported sound but not touch sensitivities. Importantly, tonotopy is a core organizational feature of auditory cortex that develops early in life and remains relatively stable after the critical period of heightened plasticity ends. Thus, these results suggest that atypical auditory processing in autism may result from early disruption to tonotopic map formation. Longitudinal neuroimaging studies are needed to understand the genetic and environmental causes of altered auditory cortex topology and its long-term consequences for higher-level auditory, language, and social communication development.

papers.title: Global statistical constraint and local partner-sensitive inference support dynamic, open-ended verbal coordination
papers.abstract: Effective verbal communication requires individuals to align their communicative intentions through the precise use of utterances, yet how this is achieved in dynamic, open-ended communication remains unclear. Combining predictive deep language models (DLMs) with cognitive computational modeling, we tested a computational division of labor between context-sensitive global constraint on the utterance space and partner-sensitive local adjustment of selection priorities. We formalized local adjustment using an active inference inspired updating rule within a statistical-pragmatic hybrid model. Thirty dyads performed a dynamic, open-ended collaborative word-generation task during functional near infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) hyperscanning. Interlocutors converged in their lexical choices, and lexical alignment was best explained by a hybrid model integrating contextual selection priors with interaction-specific local adjustment among the models tested. This hybrid process formed a dynamic hypothesis landscape comprising a global semantic search region and local selection priorities. Critically, interaction did not simply reduce uncertainty: within individuals, the hypothesis space of global semantic search progressively narrowed while local uncertainty among plausible alternatives increased; between partners, both global hypothesis space and local selection became increasingly aligned, with alignment of local selection priorities most strongly predicting subsequent lexical alignment. The contribution of local adjustment was stronger during precise verbal communication than in the control tasks. Neural analyses further identified correlates of the local adjustment process: temporoparietal and anterior temporal regions supported partner-related inference and semantic prediction error, respectively, and their activity during thinking predicted subsequent inferior frontal activity associated with self-updating during speaking. The participant's own hypothesis landscape was also represented in the left inferior parietal-supramarginal cortex. The main findings generalized across language models and an independent Czech dataset. Together, these findings reveal that alignment in open-ended communication emerges from complementary statistical and pragmatic computations, providing a framework for understanding human and human-AI communication.

papers.title: GLARE: Genomic Language model for Automated Repetitive Element classification
papers.abstract: Reliable classification of transposable elements (TEs) is important for genome annotation and evolutionary analysis, yet remains challenging: TE families differ widely across taxa, reference databases label them inconsistently, and many TEs are represented only by degraded copies. We introduce GLARE (Genomic Language model for Automated Repetitive Element classification), a TE classifier built by fine-tuning a genomic language model on harmonized PanTEon and Repbase reference data to predict TE superfamily across 32 superfamilies in 11 orders. Among the genomic language models compared, Nucleotide Transformer v3 provided the strongest representation. Built on this backbone, GLARE exceeded all nine classifiers in the PanTEon benchmark, reaching 0.966 weighted superfamily F1 on its 30-superfamily task. GLARE also showed stronger generalization to clades absent from training, consistently exceeding state-of-the-art classifiers on holdouts spanning three taxonomic ranks: the order Poales, the phylum Arthropoda, and the kingdom Fungi. Training on both PanTEon and Repbase reduced the performance drop seen when a single-source model was applied to the other database. Under simulated sequence decay, GLARE was the most robust classifier tested, and it performed best on independently curated degraded libraries. These findings show that genomic language models fine-tuned on harmonized multi-source references can classify TEs robustly under the taxonomic, database, and sequence-quality shifts that matter in practice. GLARE is available at https://code.jgi.doe.gov/NHaas/glare.

papers.title: KEDROS: A Comparative Genomics and High-Resolution Phylogenetic Profiling Workspace
papers.abstract: Phylogenetic profiling infers gene function from the presence and absence of genes across genomes, but it loses resolution in eukaryotes, where many protein families contain several functionally distinct paralogs. Existing resources address parts of this problem separately: web services build trees for one family at a time, orthology databases provide precomputed orthologous groups for predefined species sets, and tree-profiling tools require users to supply their own trees and groupings. Here, we present KEDROS, a web platform that builds gene trees for any protein family across UniProt reference proteomes, splits each tree into subfamilies at inferred gene duplications, and profiles each subfamily separately. The organisms, the families and the taxonomic depth at which trees are split are all chosen by the user, so the same workflow serves any question that can be posed as a contrast between two sets of organisms: a pathogen and its host, a pest and non-target species, or lineages with and without a trait. KEDROS answers such contrasts at two levels. Across families and subfamilies, it ranks those present in one set and absent from the other, pointing to lineage-specific genes and candidate targets. Within a subfamily shared by both sets, it identifies amino acid positions that differ consistently between them and may underlie functional divergence, and displays them on AlphaFold structures. All analyses run in a web browser, with no installation or programming. Each of these steps exists in some form elsewhere, but to our knowledge no other resource runs them end to end, at the scale of whole proteomes, on organism sets defined by the user. We illustrate KEDROS with two cases. In the trypanothione reductase family of trypanosomatids, it recovers parasite-specific subfamilies and the substrate-binding substitutions that separate the parasite enzyme from human glutathione reductase. In the bacterial phylum Bacillota, it recovers the sporulation machinery from phenotype labels alone across 1,218 proteomes, and ranks an uncharacterized family among the strongest markers of the trait. KEDROS thus offers a general, code-free route from a comparative question to testable hypotheses about genes and residues. KEDROS is freely available at https://kedros.cgenomicslab.org.

papers.title: Spoken language comprehension relies on context-dependent neural weighting of syntax and prosody
papers.abstract: Comprehending spoken language requires extracting syntactic structure and meaning from a continuous acoustic signal. Psycholinguistic evidence points to a key role for prosody in this process. However, because interactions between prosody and syntax are typically demonstrated using carefully controlled sentence constructions, it remains unclear whether such interactions constitute a general, default property of spoken language processing. Addressing this question requires naturalistic, broad-coverage data. Here, we combined experimental psycholinguistics with naturalistic neuroscience to investigate the joint neural encoding of syntax and prosody in MEG recordings of 26 participants (19 female) listening to narrative speech. Linguistic annotations revealed that strong prosodic boundaries tend to coincide with syntactic phrase closures, and that the strength of prosodic boundaries scales with the number of phrases closed. Using time-resolved regression with temporal response functions, we modeled how these features relate to delta-band neural activity during continuous speech processing. Our results reveal a bidirectional interaction between syntax and prosody. Prosodic marking modulates the neural processing of syntax, with phrase closures being encoded more strongly when accompanied by strong prosodic boundaries. Conversely, syntactic structure shapes prosodic encoding, such that boundary strength is neurally encoded primarily at points of syntactic phrase closure. These findings demonstrate that syntax and prosody are encoded not independently, but in a context-dependent and mutually constraining manner, highlighting their joint role in guiding structure building during naturalistic spoken language comprehension.

papers.title: Autonomous AI agents discover reverse transcriptases with tandem repeat arrays
papers.abstract: Metagenomic databases hold vast quantities of unexplored genetic material that can seed tools for biotechnology and medicine, but discovery is limited by our ability to examine sequence data at scale. Here, we show that large language models (LLMs) in an autonomous harness can alleviate this bottleneck and surface novel molecular systems. We deployed Claude Code instances to survey reverse transcriptase (RT) loci across 1.9 billion protein clusters. Among the top candidates were array-associated RTs (ART), a novel family of jumbo-phage RTs coupled with an array of ~200-nucleotide units and a dedicated partner gene. Session transcripts show that Claude identified the ART family by directly examining its DNA sequences and recognizing the atypical repeats, a behavior attributable to specific Mythos 5 internal signals that respond to repeated DNA. ART arrays are highly expressed and appear as discrete units during Staphylococcus phage infection, suggesting an RT system directed by a repertoire of distinct RNAs. These findings indicate that LLMs can autonomously detect anomalies and drive analyses to initiate biological discoveries.

papers.title: An Expert-Curated Benchmark for Frontier and Local LLMs Querying a Biomedical Knowledge Graph
papers.abstract: We combine GeneNetwork's 1TB structured database with its metadata as an RDF graph and an associated literature corpus. We benchmark frontier and local LLMs querying it through four architectures: document, graph and agentic retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and a combination of the three. We evaluate them on 40 domain specific expert-curated questions with a new metric: the satisfaction frequency psi (psi, i.e, the share of questions answered with precision and recall of at least 70% or an f1 of at least 60%). psi ranks systems the same way precision, recall and f1 -- a machine learning metric built from the harmonic mean of precision and recall -- but is easier to read and assess for humans. System architecture had a large effect: with full use of Claude Opus 4.8 the plain document RAG of our earlier GNQA system had a psi of 36% against 86% for our new combined tools. Delegating most of the work from Claude Opus 4.8 to a local model halved query costs while still reaching a psi of 59%.

papers.title: Sequence context decodes multi-state conformational heterogeneity from crystallographic B-factors
papers.abstract: Protein function is governed by conformational ensembles, yet the overwhelming majority of experimentally determined structures capture only static snapshots, leaving the multi-state heterogeneity that underlies biological activity largely inaccessible. X-ray crystallography, the dominant source of these structures, does carry one experimental proxy for motion, the atomic B-factor, but crystal packing and refinement artifacts frequently obscure its link to solution-state dynamics. Here we show that sequence context is sufficient to decode a protein's multi-state conformational heterogeneity from this seemingly noisy signal. We introduce the B-Factor Corrector (BFC), a fine-tuned protein language model that reframes B-factor analysis from a purely physical calculation into a sequence-context-aware translation task. By leveraging deep contextual embeddings to decouple intrinsic conformational heterogeneity from lattice constraints, BFC recovers the residue-wise heterogeneity ranking derived from crystallographic structural ensembles, reproducing the normalized profile at a Pearson correlation of 0.83 while correcting the distortions that analytical formulas leave in the raw signal. We further demonstrate the utility of this sequence-inferred signal across structural-biology applications: it provides an integrable prior for molecular docking that is statistically equivalent to experimental B-factors, unmasks cryptic conformational heterogeneity essential for chaperone function, and guides the energetic refinement of antibody interfaces to resolve steric conflicts. These results suggest that the static structures of the Protein Data Bank can be effectively repurposed to decode the conformational heterogeneity latent within them.

papers.title: CodonBench: separating gene context, exon position, and variant-specific component in synonymous-variant classification
papers.abstract: Background. A synonymous variant leaves the protein unchanged, so a classifier that still separates pathogenic from benign examples must be reading something beyond the protein. Such variants test cleanly what a codon-level model adds to a protein-level one. Methods. We assembled SynPath, a benchmark of ClinVar synonymous variants, and scored frozen representations under two splitting protocols. Under gene-held-out folds whole genes are withheld, and each coding-sequence model is compared against a position-matched control. Results. The models were not trained for this task, so these numbers describe transfer, not designed performance. Random splitting flatters every representation. Once whole genes are held out, they fall into a narrow band near chance, the best at 0.58, and low-rank fine-tuning does not restore the random-split level. A feature that reads no sequence, only the distance from the variant to the nearest exon junction, reaches 0.84 under the same folds, above every neural representation tested. In a protein model the variant-specific component is zero by construction, because both alleles present the same input. In coding-sequence models only the response vector, the difference between the alternate and reference embeddings, keeps signal on unseen genes and beats its position-matched control. Conclusions. Synonymous-variant pathogenicity is predictable mainly from gene identity and from position. Only a small part reflects the variant itself, and only in models that read the coding sequence. Benchmarks judged on random splits will overstate what these models have learned.

papers.title: AmyloCore-ML: AI/Machine Learning Enabled Identification of Amyloid Fibril Core Regions Using Protein Language Models
papers.abstract: Identification of amyloid forming regions in proteins remains central to understanding of their aggregation behaviour, which are central to various neurodegenerative and systemic disorders. Many predictors have been designed to identify amyloid forming regions, however they may not necessarily identify total residues found in actual disease associated fibril structures. To address this, we formed a sequence-based based predictor-AmyloCore-ML to ascertain structural amyloid-core propensity. The predictor was developed using experimentally determined fibril structures obtained from Amyloid Atlas. Ordered residues in the experimental structures were designated as core, and unresolved sampled from the same proteins as matched controls as non-core. Core and non-core regions were encoded using various physicochemical descriptors and protein language model (PLM) embeddings (ESM-2, ANKH, ProtT5) and evaluated using protein-grouped cross-validation. PLMs consistently outperformed physicochemical descriptors, with the best models reaching AUROC values of ~0.88 and AUPRC values of ~0.85. Locked full-length protein scans further localized experimental cores, with ESM-2/ExtraTrees achieving AUROC 0.833, AUPRC 0.751, and a mean peak distance of 12.4 residues. In comparative benchmarking, our predictor showed better performance metrics than CrossBeta and AggrescanAI. The framework therefore provides residue-resolved prediction of structurally incorporated amyloid-core regions directly from sequence.

papers.title: Computation or Weight Adaptation? Rethinking the Role of Plasticity in Learning
papers.abstract: The human brain is an adaptive learning system that can generalize to new tasks and unfamiliar environments. The traditional view is that such adaptive behavior requires a structural change of the learning system (e.g., via neural plasticity). In this work, we use artificial neural networks, specifically large language models (LLMs), to challenge this traditional view and suggest that such adaptive behavior can be also achieved solely through computation if the learning system is sufficiently trained. We focus on statistical learning paradigms. These require identifying underlying regularities in seemingly arbitrary word sequences and are primarily considered to require neural plasticity. LLMs can capture arbitrary structures without requiring weight adaptation, despite divergence from their natural language training data. Our work provides novel insights into the role of plasticity in learning, demonstrating that sufficiently trained learning systems are highly flexible, adapting to new tasks and environments solely through computation, much more than previously acknowledged. Furthermore, our work opens the door for future research to use deep learning models to conjure hypotheses about the brain.

papers.title: Inherent limitations of zero-shot mutation prediction in protein engineering
papers.abstract: Predicting mutation effects is critical for protein engineering. A commonly pursued strategy is zero-shot prediction with deep-learning models, whose performance is typically evaluated using aggregate benchmark scores that obscure multidimensional biological tradeoffs. Here, we evaluate sequence, structure, and hybrid foundation models across curated datasets to expose the practical limitations of zero-shot predictions. We demonstrate that model performance is highly variable and heavily influenced by experimental noise and competing phenotypic goals. Notably, predictions from competing models often correlate more strongly with one another than with experimental outcomes. While current models effectively filter deleterious mutations and enrich high-scoring variants for natural functions, they struggle to identify precise optimal mutations and consistently fail to predict mutations that drive new-to-nature functions. These models learn from evolutionary constraints that tend to oppose the extreme biophysical optimizations required in targeted engineering. Consequently, zero-shot scoring serves as a valuable initial filter but cannot substitute for task-specific prediction.

papers.title: Spatial proteomics identifies altered thick ascending limb cells as drivers of kidney disease through uromodulin retention
papers.abstract: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is increasingly prevalent and is a leading cause of mortality. Recent transcriptomic studies have identified the persistence of injury-induced renal tubular epithelial cell states, yet the cell populations that drive CKD remain unresolved. Uromodulin (UMOD) is the most abundant urinary secreted protein expressed exclusively in thick ascending limb (TAL) epithelial cells in the kidney. UMOD is strongly associated with CKD risk in genome-wide association studies, suggesting a broader, yet unexplored role of UMOD and TAL cells in CKD pathogenesis. Here, using spatial proteomics, we identified an injury-induced TAL cell state marked by intracellular UMOD accumulation. Spatially resolved multimodal integration revealed that UMOD accumulation occurred without transcriptional upregulation. Impaired urinary UMOD secretion further supported pathological intracellular retention. These altered TAL cells with UMOD retention exhibited inflammatory signaling, formed profibrotic niches enriched with M2-like macrophages across renal compartments, and were associated with CKD progression in multiple experimental models. Reducing the burden of UMOD retention diminished altered TAL cells and their profibrotic microenvironments, and attenuated CKD development. A similar altered TAL state was identified in human kidney disease and was associated with worse kidney function. Together, we identify pathological UMOD retention and altered TAL cells as key drivers of CKD development and potential therapeutic targets. This study also highlights that protein-level alterations can redefine disease-associated cell states beyond transcript profiling.

papers.title: Representing biological concepts as directions in foundation model embeddings
papers.abstract: Biological foundation models encode rich information about protein structure, function, and cellular state in high-dimensional embeddings, but accessing specific biological properties typically relies on additional, task-specific prediction models. Here, we show that diverse biological properties can be mapped to interpretable, reusable directions in embedding space. In the Concept Activation Vector (CAV) approach, examples representing a concept are distinguished from a background set using a linear model, and the resulting weight vector defines the CAV for that concept. In protein embeddings, CAVs recover Gene Ontology and Enzyme Commission annotations, localize Pfam domains, reveal novel structural relationships, and capture DNA-binding and protein-interaction interface specificity. In single-cell embeddings, CAVs isolate cancer-associated expression transitions, and gene variation along these axes substantially agrees with conventional differential-expression analysis despite being a distinct computational approach. Together, these results establish concept directions as a common representation, enabling diverse biological features to be compared, localized, and manipulated.
